content: Vegetarian cuisine is defined as food that adheres to vegetarian standards by excluding meat and animal tissue products. In lacto-ovo vegetarianism, which is the most prevalent form of vegetarianism in Western countries, dairy products such as eggs, milk, and cheese are allowed. Veganism, the strictest form of vegetarianism, excludes all animal-derived products, including dairy, honey, and even some refined sugars that are processed using bone char. Vegetarian foods can be categorized into two main types: traditional vegetarian foods, which have always been plant-based (e.g., cereals, grains, fruits, vegetables, nuts), and meat analogues, which are designed to replicate the taste, texture, and appearance of meat. These analogues are often used in recipes that traditionally include meat. Vegans may also use substitutes for eggs and dairy products, such as tofu and textured vegetable protein (TVP), which are common examples of these analogues. Foods Commonly Used in Vegetarian Cuisine Vegetarian cuisine typically includes a wide variety of plant-based ingredients: Cereals and grains: Examples include maize, corn, wheat, rice, barley, sorghum, millet, oats, rye, triticale, buckwheat, fonio, and quinoa, along with their derived products like flour, bread, pasta, and baked goods. Vegetables and mushrooms: These can be consumed fresh or pickled, and derived products like vegetable fats and oils are also included. However, some strict Indian vegetarians avoid mushrooms. Fruits: Both fresh and dried fruits are widely consumed. Legumes: This category includes beans (such as soybeans and their derivatives like tofu, soy milk, and TVP), chickpeas, peas, lentils, and peanuts. Tree nuts and seeds: These are common sources of protein and fats. Spices and herbs: Widely used to enhance flavor. Other plant-based foods: Examples include olives and seaweed. Dairy products: Milk, butter, cheese, and yogurt are included in lacto-ovo vegetarian diets but are excluded in vegan diets. Traditional Vegetarian Dishes Many dishes are inherently vegetarian and do not require ingredient substitutions. These include: Pasta, rice, bean, potato, and bulgur/couscous dishes, as well as stews, soups, and stir-fries. Breakfast items like cereals, oatmeal, granola bars, and donuts. Fresh fruits and most salads. Side dishes such as mashed potatoes, scalloped potatoes, seasoned rice, and macaroni and cheese. Sandwiches like grilled cheese or those made with roasted eggplant, mushrooms, bell peppers, avocado, and other vegetarian fillings. Classic Buddhist cuisine served in Asian temples, which is strictly vegetarian. National Vegetarian Cuisines Certain national cuisines are rich in vegetarian dishes: Indian cuisine: Vegetarianism is deeply rooted in religious traditions, such as those of Hindu Brahmins. Common vegetarian dishes include pakora, samosa, khichri, pulao, raitas, rasam, chana masala, saag aloo, and various South Indian foods like dosas, idlis, and vadas. Many Indian dishes are also vegan, though some use dairy or honey. Spanish cuisine: Includes dishes like tumbet, polentas, and various tapas. Mexican cuisine: Vegetarian options include salsa and guacamole with chips, rice and bean burritos (without lard or chicken fat), bean tacos, cheese enchiladas, and vegetable fajitas. Italian cuisine: Many pastas, pizzas, risottos, and dishes like eggplant parmigiana and bruschetta are vegetarian. Continental cuisine: Includes ratatouille, braised leeks, quiches, and vegetable-stuffed mushrooms. Balkan cuisine: Features dishes like dolmas and spanakopita. Russian and Slavic cuisine: Includes vegetable borscht, pirogi, blini, and fermented vegetables. Ethiopian cuisine: Offers a variety of vegetarian dishes. Middle Eastern cuisine: Includes falafel, hummus, tahini, and couscous. Chinese cuisine: Features dishes based on mushrooms, noodles, eggplant, string beans, broccoli, rice, and tofu. Japanese cuisine: Includes vegetable sushi, tempura, and miso soup, though vegetarian in Japan may still include fish. Thai cuisine: Offers vegetarian options like pad kee mao and Thai curries. Creole and Southern cuisine: Includes dishes like hush puppies, okra patties, and rice and beans, provided they are not cooked with pork fat or meat stock. Welsh cuisine: Includes dishes like Glamorgan sausages and Welsh rarebit. Desserts Many desserts are naturally vegetarian, such as pies, cobblers, cakes, brownies, cookies, truffles, rice pudding, and ice cream. Oriental confections like halva and Turkish delight are often vegan, while baklava is at least vegetarian. Cuisine Using Meat Analogues Vegetarian versions of popular meat-based dishes are widely available and often consumed as fast food, comfort food, or transitional food for new vegetarians. Examples include: Mock meats or meaty balls made from TVP. Vegetarian or meatless chicken made from seitan, tofu, or TVP. Jambalaya with mock sausage and chicken, often made from TVP, seitan, or tempeh. Tomato omelettes made with a flour paste instead of eggs. Scrambled tofu, seasoned with spices like turmeric to mimic the appearance and flavor of scrambled eggs. Mycoprotein is another common base for mock meats, with vegetarian flavorings added to replicate seafood or other tastes. Ingredients like tempeh and tofu are also used in their own right in various cuisines, not just as meat substitutes.
